claim: Conspecific negative density dependence is ubiquitous and has long been recognized as an important factor favoring the coexistence of competing species at local scale.
source: Conspecific negative density dependence is ubiquitous and has long been recognized as an important factor favoring the coexistence of competing species at local scale.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in ecology, drawing from the broader literature on density dependence and coexistence theory.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence is thought to favor species exclusion by inhibiting the growth of less competitive species.
source: By contrast, a positive density-dependent growth rate is thought to favor species exclusion by inhibiting the growth of less competitive species.
evidence: This represents the prevailing theoretical understanding in the field, as supported by citations to Wang et al., 1999 and De Silva and Jang, 2015 elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence often reduces extrinsic mortality (e.g. reduced predation).
source: Yet, such conspecific positive density dependence often reduces extrinsic mortality (e.g. reduced predation), which favors species exclusion in the first place.
evidence: This is supported by the examples and mechanisms described in Figure 1 and Figure 2, as well as citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence acting on mortality can favor the existence of equilibrium points characterized by species coexistence.
source: Here, using a combination of analytical derivations and numerical simulations, I show that this form of positive density dependence can favor the existence of equilibrium points characterized by species coexistence.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by analytical derivations (Equations 1a-1b, Figure 4, Figure 5) and numerical simulations (Figure 6, Figure 7).

claim: Coexistence equilibria under conspecific positive density dependence acting on mortality are not globally stable.
source: Those equilibria are not globally stable, but allow the maintenance of species-rich communities in multispecies simulations.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analytical analysis showing local but not global stability (Figure 4, Figure 5) and numerical simulations (Figure 6).

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence acting on mortality allows the maintenance of species-rich communities in multispecies simulations.
source: Those equilibria are not globally stable, but allow the maintenance of species-rich communities in multispecies simulations.
evidence: This is supported by the multispecies simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Some forms of conspecific positive density dependence may help maintain species richness in natural communities.
source: On the contrary, some forms of conspecific positive density dependence may even help maintain species richness in natural communities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results and represents a speculative extension to natural systems.

claim: Species richness in a local community is the result of several processes that act at different scales, none of them being mutually exclusive.
source: Species richness in a local community is the result of several processes that act at different scales, none of them being mutually exclusive (Götzenberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Götzenberger et al., 2012 and represents established ecological theory.

claim: At regional and global scales, randomness and dispersal processes affect species richness.
source: At regional and global scales, these include randomness and dispersal processes (Hubbell, 2001; Leibold and Chase, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hubbell, 2001 and Leibold and Chase, 2018.

claim: At local scale, biotic interactions determine community assembly in addition to abiotic factors.
source: At local scale, in addition to abiotic factors (physical constraints of the environment), biotic interactions determine community assembly (Gause, 1934; Hutchinson, 1961; Holt, 1977; Tilman, 1982; Chesson, 2000; Gross, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational ecological literature.

claim: Competitive imbalances can lead to the exclusion of less competitive species.
source: In particular, some species are better competitors than others, and competitive imbalances can lead to the exclusion of less competitive species (Gause, 1934; Levin, 1970; Tilman, 1982; Meszéna et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic competition theory literature.

claim: Interspecific competition for resources has been recognized as one of the main drivers of species exclusion.
source: Interspecific competition for resources (see Box 1 for a glossary of terms in italics) has been recognized as one of the main drivers of species exclusion (Gause, 1934; Tilman, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gause, 1934 and Tilman, 1982.

claim: Interspecific reproductive interference can inhibit species coexistence.
source: Additionally, interspecific reproductive interference – i.e. any interspecific sexual interaction reducing the reproductive success of females – can inhibit species coexistence.
evidence: This is supported by theoretical and empirical citations provided in the subsequent sentence.

claim: Interspecific sexual interactions are common in nature, especially among closely related species.
source: Such interspecific sexual interactions are common in nature, especially among closely related species (Gröning and Hochkirch, 2008), and can cause species exclusion more easily than competition for resources, as shown theoretically (Kuno, 1992; Yoshimura and Clark, 1994; Kishi and Nakazawa, 2013; Schreiber et al., 2019) and empirically in some species (Takafuji et al., 1997; Kishi et al., 2009; Takakura et al., 2009; Crowder et al., 2010; Crowder et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gröning and Hochkirch, 2008 and multiple theoretical and empirical studies.

claim: Reproductive interference can cause species exclusion more easily than competition for resources.
source: Such interspecific sexual interactions are common in nature, especially among closely related species (Gröning and Hochkirch, 2008), and can cause species exclusion more easily than competition for resources, as shown theoretically (Kuno, 1992; Yoshimura and Clark, 1994; Kishi and Nakazawa, 2013; Schreiber et al., 2019) and empirically in some species (Takafuji et al., 1997; Kishi et al., 2009; Takakura et al., 2009; Crowder et al., 2010; Crowder et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by both theoretical and empirical citations.

claim: Many mechanisms favoring species coexistence have been identified, including niche separation, predatory/herbivory interactions, positive interactions, crowding effects, and individual-level variations.
source: In the face of these negative interspecific interactions, many mechanisms favoring species coexistence have been identified. These include niche separation (Gause, 1934), predatory/herbivory interactions (Chesson and Huntly, 1997), positive interactions (Gross, 2008), crowding effects (Gavina et al., 2018), and individual-level variations (Uriarte and Menge, 2018; but see Hart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on coexistence mechanisms.

claim: Species often differ in their use of multiple-limiting resources, causing species to limit their own population growths more than they limit others.
source: Notably, species often differ in their use of multiple-limiting resources (Tilman, 1982), causing species to limit their own population growths more than they limit others (Adler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tilman, 1982 and Adler et al., 2007.

claim: A core tenet of Chesson's coexistence theory is that negative density dependence must be stronger among conspecifics than among heterospecifics for species to coexist in two-species systems.
source: A core tenet of Chesson's coexistence theory – one of the well-developed coexistence theories – is precisely that negative density dependence must be stronger among conspecifics (conspecific negative density dependence) than among heterospecifics (heterospecific negative density dependence) for species to coexist in two-species systems (Chesson, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chesson, 2000.

claim: The criterion that conspecific negative density dependence must be stronger than heterospecific negative density dependence does not hold in multispecies communities.
source: Even though this criterion does not hold in multispecies communities (Barabás et al., 2016; Song et al., 2019), the importance of conspecific negative density dependence – when the growth rate of a population decreases as its density increases – for species coexistence in two-species systems is well accepted (MacArthur, 1970; Chesson, 2000; McPeek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barabás et al., 2016 and Song et al., 2019.

claim: The importance of conspecific negative density dependence for species coexistence in two-species systems is well accepted.
source: Even though this criterion does not hold in multispecies communities (Barabás et al., 2016; Song et al., 2019), the importance of conspecific negative density dependence – when the growth rate of a population decreases as its density increases – for species coexistence in two-species systems is well accepted (MacArthur, 1970; Chesson, 2000; McPeek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacArthur, 1970; Chesson, 2000; and McPeek, 2012.

claim: Conspecific negative density dependence favors the existence of a coexistence equilibrium that is globally stable.
source: Indeed, conspecific negative density dependence favors the existence of a coexistence equilibrium (i.e. the 'feasibility condition' is fulfilled) that is globally stable (all species can invade even if they are rare initially; i.e. the 'global stability condition' is fulfilled) (Case, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Case, 2000.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence can inhibit the coexistence of species interacting negatively with each other by reducing the growth rate of inferior competitors that are at lower density than superior competitors.
source: Contrary to conspecific negative density dependence, conspecific positive density dependence can inhibit the coexistence of species interacting negatively with each other (e.g. via competition for resources or reproductive interference) by reducing even further the growth rate of inferior competitors that are at lower density than superior competitors (as shown theoretically by Wang et al., 1999 and De Silva and Jang, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 1999 and De Silva and Jang, 2015.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence can constrain the conditions under which there is stable coexistence (the feasibility condition).
source: More precisely, the effect of conspecific positive density dependence on coexistence is two-fold. First, it can constrain the conditions under which there is stable coexistence (i.e. the 'feasibility condition' is constrained).
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical literature cited (Wang et al., 1999; De Silva and Jang, 2015).

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence can inhibit the invasion of species that are at low density initially (the global stability condition is unfulfilled).
source: Second, it can inhibit the invasion of species that are at low density initially (i.e. the 'global stability condition' is unfulfilled).
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical literature and is demonstrated in the study's own results.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence, in concert with competition for resources and reproductive interference, can be a potent mechanism inhibiting the coexistence of competing species.
source: Therefore, in concert with competition for resources and reproductive interference, conspecific positive density dependence can be a potent mechanism inhibiting the coexistence of competing species.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical understanding described in the preceding sentences.

claim: Heterospecific positive density dependence has been documented and can promote species coexistence.
source: Note that heterospecific positive density dependence – when the growth rate of a population increases as the density of heterospecifics increases – has also been documented (it can arise from any mutualistic interaction; for example Bruno et al., 2003) and can promote species coexistence (Gross, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bruno et al., 2003 and Gross, 2008.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence has been described for most major animal taxa.
source: Conspecific positive density dependence has been described for most major animal taxa (reviewed by Courchamp et al., 1999; Stephens et al., 1999; Kramer et al., 2009), and can be caused by a variety of mechanisms, such as mate limitation (Gascoigne et al., 2009), cooperative feeding (Carbone et al., 1997), cooperative defense (Angulo et al., 2018), predator satiation (Gascoigne and Lipcius, 2004) or anti-predator strategies (like aposematism, Mallet and Joron, 1999; Joron and Iwasa, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review papers and empirical studies.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence can be caused by mate limitation, cooperative feeding, cooperative defense, predator satiation, or anti-predator strategies.
source: Conspecific positive density dependence has been described for most major animal taxa (reviewed by Courchamp et al., 1999; Stephens et al., 1999; Kramer et al., 2009), and can be caused by a variety of mechanisms, such as mate limitation (Gascoigne et al., 2009), cooperative feeding (Carbone et al., 1997), cooperative defense (Angulo et al., 2018), predator satiation (Gascoigne and Lipcius, 2004) or anti-predator strategies (like aposematism, Mallet and Joron, 1999; Joron and Iwasa, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies on each mechanism.

claim: In plants, conspecific positive density dependence can be driven by inbreeding depression, pollen limitation, or substrate modification.
source: In plants, conspecific positive density dependence can be driven by inbreeding depression (Willi et al., 2005), pollen limitation (Sih and Baltus, 1987; Groom, 1998) or substrate modification (favoring seedling establishment, Bruno et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on plant mechanisms.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence can associate with increased reproduction or reduced mortality.
source: Interestingly, conspecific positive dependence can associate with increased reproduction or reduced mortality (Figure 1; as emphasized by Berec et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1 and citation to Berec et al., 2007.

claim: Theoretical models investigating the determinants of species coexistence have considered conspecific positive density dependence acting on birth rates or net growth rates, but not on mortality rates alone.
source: However, theoretical models investigating the determinants of species coexistence have considered conspecific positive density dependence acting on birth rates (Wang et al., 1999) or net growth rates (defined as the difference between birth rate and mortality rate; De Silva and Jang, 2015), but not on mortality rates alone.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 1999 and De Silva and Jang, 2015, and represents a gap in the literature that this study addresses.

claim: Decreased mortality rates at high population density give rise to conspecific positive density dependence in many species.
source: Decreased mortality rates at high population density give rise to conspecific positive density dependence in many species (Figure 1; and see the description of specific natural history examples in Figure 2), yet the effect of this form of conspecific positive density dependence on species coexistence has not been investigated explicitly.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1 and Figure 2 showing examples from multiple taxa.

claim: The effect of conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality on species coexistence has not been investigated explicitly.
source: Decreased mortality rates at high population density give rise to conspecific positive density dependence in many species (Figure 1; and see the description of specific natural history examples in Figure 2), yet the effect of this form of conspecific positive density dependence on species coexistence has not been investigated explicitly.
evidence: This represents a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: Density-dependent mechanisms can counteract with each other.
source: Indeed, it is important to remember that different mechanisms leading to density dependence can occur simultaneously in the same population (Berec et al., 2007). In particular, density-dependent mechanisms can counteract with each other (Feldman and Morris, 2011; Bergamo et al., 2020), and observing an overall pattern of negative density dependence does not mean that some forms of positive density dependence do not take place.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berec et al., 2007; Feldman and Morris, 2011; and Bergamo et al., 2020.

claim: Observing an overall pattern of negative density dependence does not mean that some forms of positive density dependence do not take place.
source: In particular, density-dependent mechanisms can counteract with each other (Feldman and Morris, 2011; Bergamo et al., 2020), and observing an overall pattern of negative density dependence does not mean that some forms of positive density dependence do not take place.
evidence: This is an inference from the understanding that multiple density-dependent mechanisms can operate simultaneously.

claim: Heliconius butterflies are aposematic and benefit from reduced predation when conspecifics are abundant.
source: (a) Heliconius butterflies are aposematic (toxic and conspicuous) and therefore benefit from reduced predation when conspecifics are abundant.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2 and illustrated in the figure.

claim: Black-browed albatrosses in large flocks benefit from increased foraging efficiency and therefore from increased survival.
source: (b) Black-browed albatrosses in large flocks benefits from increased foraging efficiency and therefore from increased survival (Grünbaum and Veit, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grünbaum and Veit, 2003 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Bottlebrush squirreltail in high density have a high survival rate and a high establishment success in arid grasslands.
source: (c) Bottlebrush squirreltail in high density have a high survival rate and a high establishement success in arid grasslands (Sheley and James, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sheley and James, 2014 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Meerkats in large groups benefit from increased vigilance at the group level, reducing the risk of predation.
source: (d) Meerkats in large group benefit from increased vigilance at the group level, reducing the risk of predation (Clutton-Brock et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clutton-Brock et al., 1999 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Wild dogs in large groups benefit from high hunting success and defend effectively their kill against kleptoparasitism, thereby increasing their survival.
source: (e) Wild dogs in large group benefit from a high hunting success and defend effectively their kill against kleptoparasitism, thereby increasing their survival (Fanshawe and Fitzgibbon, 1993; Carbone et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fanshawe and Fitzgibbon, 1993 and Carbone et al., 1997, and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Ribbed mussels in high density benefit from reduced crab predation and from improved winter ice resistance.
source: (f) Ribbed mussels in high density benefit from reduced crab predation and from improved winter ice resistance (Bertness and Grosholz, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bertness and Grosholz, 1985 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality also changes the overall magnitude of extrinsic mortality.
source: Nonetheless, density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality (e.g. density-dependent predation) also changes the overall magnitude of extrinsic mortality, yet extrinsic mortality can inhibit species coexistence in the first place (as shown by Holt, 1985, using the global stability criterion).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holt, 1985.

claim: Extrinsic mortality can inhibit species coexistence.
source: Nonetheless, density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality (e.g. density-dependent predation) also changes the overall magnitude of extrinsic mortality, yet extrinsic mortality can inhibit species coexistence in the first place (as shown by Holt, 1985, using the global stability criterion).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holt, 1985.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence acting only on mortality may yield a different outcome in terms of species coexistence compared to positive density dependence acting on birth rates.
source: For this reason, conspecific positive density dependence acting only on mortality may yield to a different outcome in term of species coexistence.
evidence: This is an inference that motivates the study's investigation.

claim: A locally stable coexistence equilibrium often exists under conspecific positive density dependence acting on mortality in a two-species model with asymmetric resource competition.
source: First, I analyze analytically a two-species model with asymmetric resource competition and conspecific positive density dependence acting on mortality, and I show that a locally stable coexistence equilibrium often exists under such positive density dependence.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analytical derivations presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence acting on mortality substantially increases the coexistence region in models accounting for differences in basal mortality or asymmetric reproductive interference.
source: Second, using numerically simulations, I show that this form of conspecific positive density dependence substantially increases the coexistence region in models accounting for other forms of species asymmetry, as differences in basal mortality (in addition to symmetric resource competition) or asymmetric reproductive interference.
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence generally inhibits the global stability of coexistence but can increase the feasibility domain of the coexistence equilibrium.
source: In other words, this form of conspecific positive density dependence generally inhibits the global stability of coexistence but can also increase the feasibility domain of the coexistence equilibrium.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the analytical and numerical results shown in Figure 4, Figure 5, and Figure 6.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality can maintain species-rich communities in multispecies simulations.
source: Third, using simulations of a multi- (> 2) species model, I then show that conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality can thereby maintain species-rich communities.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multispecies simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both species in the two-species model with asymmetric competition are assumed to exhibit conspecific negative density dependence due to competition for resources.
source: Both species are assumed to exhibit conspecific negative density dependence due to competition for resources, such that changes in abundances are chosen as logistic regulation rules.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in the methods.

claim: In the two-species model with asymmetric competition, the presence of species 1 inhibits the growth of species 2, whereas species 2 has no effect on the growth of species 1.
source: Additionally, the presence of species 1 inhibits the growth of species 2, whereas species 2 has no effect on the growth of species 1 – i.e. there is asymmetric interspecific competition for resources leading to heterospecific negative density dependence in one species only.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in the methods and reflected in Equations 1a.

claim: In the two-species model with asymmetric competition, species are assumed to be similar aside from asymmetric competition.
source: Aside from asymmetric competition, species are assumed to be similar in order to keep the model analytically tractable. In particular, species have the same carrying capacity, and the growth of both species is constrained by the same type of conspecific density dependence (same conspecific negative density dependence driven by competition for resources, and same conspecific positive density dependence acting on mortality).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated in the methods.

claim: The density-dependent mortality term decreases effective intrinsic growth rates and effective carrying capacities.
source: The density-dependent mortality term decreases not only effective intrinsic growth rates, but also effective carrying capacities – i.e. density values reached at equilibrium without competitor (see Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is derived mathematically in the supplementary materials.

claim: The population dynamic of species 1 is not affected by the density of species 2 in the asymmetric competition model; only species 2 can be excluded.
source: Note that the population dynamic of species 1 is not affected by the density of species 2; only species 2 can be excluded.
evidence: This follows from the structure of Equations 1a where species 2 does not appear in the equation for species 1.

claim: When the coexistence equilibrium exists in the asymmetric competition model, it is always locally stable.
source: The coexistence equilibrium is always locally stable when it exists (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analytical stability analysis and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: At coexistence equilibrium, the least competitive species is always at lower density than the most competitive species.
source: At coexistence equilibrium, the least competitive species is always at lower density than the most competitive species (Figure 4d–f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: Increased density-dependence factor can promote the feasibility of coexistence in conditions where the least competitive species is excluded.
source: In conditions where the least competitive species is excluded, this same effect can promote the feasibility of coexistence.
evidence: This is an inference from the mechanism described and demonstrated in the results.

claim: The phenomenon where increased density-dependence factor increases feasibility of coexistence occurs when other non-linear or linear mortality functions are implemented.
source: Notably, this phenomenon occurs when other non-linear or linear mortality functions are implemented (using a numerical method validated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality can substantially increase the feasibility domain of the coexistence equilibrium when competitive exclusion is driven by other forms of species asymmetry.
source: Yet, as we shall see in the next section, conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality can substantially increase the feasibility domain of the coexistence equilibrium when competitive exclusion is driven by other forms of species asymmetry.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the numerical results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Reproductive interference is more prone to species exclusion than other forms of species asymmetry tested.
source: In particular, reproductive interference is more prone to species exclusion than the other forms of species asymmetry tested (e.g. see comparable graphs in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 vs. Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing results in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under asymmetric reproductive interference, coexistence is only ever a local attractor; the least competitive species cannot invade if it is too rare initially.
source: Likewise, under asymmetric reproductive interference which is frequency-dependent, coexistence is only ever a local attractor; the least competitive species cannot invade if it is too rare initially and the condition of global stability is never fulfilled (as shown by Kishi and Nakazawa, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kishi and Nakazawa, 2013 and demonstrated in Figure 6d-f.

claim: In models with asymmetric basal mortality and reproductive interference, conspecific positive density dependence can substantially increase the coexistence region compared to the situation without positive density dependence.
source: Here, this form of positive density dependence can substantially increase the coexistence region, compared to the situation without positive density dependence (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: The condition of global stability is never fulfilled when positive density dependence favors the feasibility of coexistence in the models with asymmetric basal mortality and reproductive interference.
source: Note, however, that the condition of global stability is never fulfilled when positive density dependence favors the feasibility of coexistence.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 where coexistence at high s is always a local attractor (gray zones).

claim: Four different scenarios are considered in the multispecies models: only asymmetric competition, only asymmetric reproductive interference, only differences in basal mortality, and random communities with all forms of asymmetry.
source: Four different scenarios are considered successively: (1) only asymmetric competition, (2) only asymmetric reproductive interference, (3) only differences in basal mortality, (4) random communities with all forms of asymmetry.
evidence: This describes the structure of the multispecies simulations.

claim: For each multispecies scenario, 500 species pools of 100 species each were constructed by drawing species parameter values from arbitrary uniform distributions.
source: For each scenario, 500 species pools of 100 species each were constructed by drawing species parameter values from arbitrary uniform distributions (detailed in Supplementary file 1D; see the robustness to variations in the uniform distributions tested in Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: In all multispecies simulations in which multiple species persisted, coexistence occurred at a stable equilibrium.
source: In all simulations in which multiple species persisted, coexistence occurred at a stable equilibrium.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation results.

claim: The density-dependence factor has a non-linear effect on species richness maintained at equilibrium in multispecies simulations.
source: Consistent with the previous two-species models, the density-dependence factor has a non-linear effect on species richness maintained at equilibrium (Figure 7a–c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7a-c.

claim: Species richness remains high under the conditions where there is a coexistence equilibrium in the two-species models, including for high density-dependence factors.
source: Indeed, species richness remains high under the conditions where there is a coexistence equilibrium in the two-species models, including for high density-dependence factors (Figure 4 and Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figure 7 with Figure 4 and Figure 6.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality can help maintain species-rich communities in multispecies models.
source: Therefore, conspecific positive density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality can help maintain species-rich communities.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the multispecies simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: In scenarios of community assembly where species are introduced one at a time at very low density, positive density dependence does not help produce species-rich communities.
source: A second set of simulations in which species were introduced one at a time produced different results. In such scenarios of community assembly, positive density dependence does not help produce species-rich communities (if species are introduced at very low density; Figure 7—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 9.

claim: The result that positive density dependence does not help in sequential assembly scenarios is consistent with the two-species models where the condition of global stability is not fulfilled for a high density-dependence factor.
source: This is consistent with the two-species models analyzed where the condition of global stability is not fulfilled for a high density-dependence factor.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the sequential assembly results to the two-species analytical results.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence acting on intrinsic growth rate can inhibit coexistence among competing species.
source: When intraspecific competition is stronger than interspecific competition, resulting negative density-dependent growth rate has long been recognized as an important factor favoring coexistence among competing species (MacArthur, 1970; Chesson, 2000; McPeek, 2012), and it is therefore not surprising that conspecific positive density dependence acting on intrinsic growth rate can inhibit coexistence among competing species (as shown theoretically by Wang et al., 1999; De Silva and Jang, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 1999 and De Silva and Jang, 2015.

claim: Different forms of conspecific positive density dependence can have opposite effects on the feasibility of species coexistence.
source: How can different forms of conspecific positive density dependence have opposite effects on the feasibility of species coexistence?
evidence: This is a rhetorical question that introduces the explanation of the study's findings.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence per se promotes species exclusion by reducing the growth rate of inferior competitors that are at lower density than superior competitors.
source: Conspecific positive density dependence per se promotes species exclusion by reducing the growth rate of inferior competitors that are at lower density than superior competitors.
evidence: This is established theory supported by the citations to Wang et al., 1999 and De Silva and Jang, 2015.

claim: Reduced mortality associated with conspecific positive density dependence can increase the feasibility domain of species coexistence.
source: However, reduced mortality associated with conspecific positive density dependence can also increase the feasibility domain of species coexistence (i.e. it can favor the existence of a locally stable equilibrium of coexistence).
evidence: This is the key finding of the study, demonstrated through the analytical and numerical results.

claim: Increased mortality can lead to the exclusion of less competitive species.
source: Increased mortality can lead to the exclusion of less competitive species (Abrams, 1977; Holt, 1985; but see Abrams, 2001), and this is the case in the two models analyzed numerically in this paper (Equations 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abrams, 1977; Holt, 1985; and Abrams, 2001, and demonstrated in the study's models.

claim: By reducing the mortality of less competitive species, conspecific positive density dependence can favor coexistence among competing species.
source: Therefore, by reducing the mortality of less competitive species, conspecific positive density dependence can favor coexistence among competing species.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic explanation for the study's findings.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence associated with an increase of mortality should favor species exclusion.
source: By contrast, conspecific positive density dependence associated with an increase of mortality should favor species exclusion (e.g. anthropogenic Allee effects; Courchamp et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference from the logic of the study, supported by citation to Courchamp et al., 2006.

claim: In cases where increased mortality increases the feasibility of coexistence, conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality should favor species exclusion.
source: Likewise, in cases where increased mortality increases the feasibility of coexistence (e.g. in a MacArthur's consumer-resource model; Abrams, 2001), conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality should also favor species exclusion.
evidence: This is an inference from the logic of the study, supported by citation to Abrams, 2001.

claim: Under conspecific positive density dependence, the least competitive species is often not able to increase in density if it is too rare.
source: Under conspecific positive density dependence, the least competitive species is often not able to increase in density if it is too rare – i.e. coexistence is only a local attractor and the condition of global stability is not fulfilled.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the study's results (Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 6).

claim: Invasibility is often considered as a fundamental criterion for species coexistence regardless of the underlying mechanism.
source: Invasibility is often considered as a fundamental criterion for species coexistence regardless of the underlying mechanism (Chesson, 2000; Siepielski and McPeek, 2010; Grainger et al., 2019); indeed, global stability of a feasible equilibrium point is a sufficient condition for species coexistence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chesson, 2000; Siepielski and McPeek, 2010; and Grainger et al., 2019.

claim: The condition of global stability is rarely fulfilled in systems with more than two species.
source: Nonetheless, the condition of global stability is rarely fulfilled in systems with more than two species, and the feasibility of coexistence has also been recognized as an important determinant of multispecies coexistence (see Saavedra et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2017; Grainger et al., 2019, for discussion on the evaluation of multispecies coexistence).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saavedra et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2017; and Grainger et al., 2019.

claim: The feasibility of coexistence has been recognized as an important determinant of multispecies coexistence.
source: Nonetheless, the condition of global stability is rarely fulfilled in systems with more than two species, and the feasibility of coexistence has also been recognized as an important determinant of multispecies coexistence (see Saavedra et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2017; Grainger et al., 2019, for discussion on the evaluation of multispecies coexistence).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saavedra et al., 2017; Levine et al., 2017; and Grainger et al., 2019.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence strongly increases the coexistence region in the two-species models analyzed numerically.
source: While the coexistence equilibria identified do not satisfy this invasibility criterion, conspecific positive density dependence strongly increases the coexistence region (i.e. the feasibility domain of coexistence) in the two-species models analyzed numerically.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: Numerical simulations of multispecies models show that conspecific positive density dependence can favor the existence of stable equilibrium points characterized by the maintenance of many competing species.
source: Moreover, numerical simulations of multispecies models show that conspecific positive density dependence can favor the existence of stable equilibrium points characterized by the maintenance of many competing species.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: Positive density dependence acting on mortality can help maintain species diversity in ecological communities.
source: This suggests that positive density dependence acting on mortality can help maintain species diversity in ecological communities.
evidence: This is an inference from the multispecies simulation results.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence can increase species densities at coexistence equilibrium.
source: However, another effect of conspecific positive dependence is to increase the species densities at coexistence equilibrium (see Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1A), and therefore to increase robustness to stochastic changes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4 and the supplementary materials.

claim: Under conspecific positive density dependence, only strong stochasticity may lead to local extinction.
source: Under conspecific positive density dependence, only strong stochasticity may lead to local extinction, yet such strong stochasticity would also favor the invasion of new species – the threshold above which a species can invade would be more easily attained by chance.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the implications of stochasticity.

claim: In the face of stochasticity, the effect of conspecific positive density dependence on species richness in metacommunities may differ from the deterministic case studied in this paper.
source: In the face of stochasticity, the effect of conspecific positive density dependence on species richness in metacommunities may therefore differ from the deterministic case studied in this paper, and therefore requires further theoretical investigations (e.g. following the approach followed by Schreiber et al., 2019, combining frequency-dependence and environmental stochasticity).
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: Putative examples of conspecific positive density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality have been described in many taxa.
source: Putative examples of conspecific positive density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality have already been described in many taxa (Figure 1 and Figure 2) (note however that difficulties in detecting negative density dependence may be similarly applied in detecting positive density-dependence; Detto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1 and Figure 2, with a caveat from Detto et al., 2019.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence acting on extrinsic mortality may play an important role in structuring certain ecological communities.
source: This form of conspecific positive density dependence may play an important role in structuring certain ecological communities.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and the examples provided.

claim: The high species richness in aposematic organisms at local scale is likely caused by conspecific positive density dependence associating with reduced mortality.
source: For instance, the high species richness that can be found in aposematic organisms at local scale (e.g. in aposematic butterflies, Willmott et al., 2017) is likely to be caused by conspecific positive density dependence associating with reduced mortality (via density-dependent predator avoidance which has received much empirical support; Ruxton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Willmott et al., 2017 and Ruxton et al., 2018.

claim: An overall pattern of negative density dependence has been observed in many plant communities.
source: By contrast, an overall pattern of negative density dependence has been observed in other ecological communities (e.g. in many plant communities; Adler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adler et al., 2018.

claim: Observing an overall pattern of negative density dependence does not mean that conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality is not pervasive in those communities.
source: This does not mean that conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality is not pervasive in those communities.
evidence: This is an inference from the understanding that multiple density-dependent mechanisms can operate simultaneously.

claim: Different mechanisms leading to density dependence can occur simultaneously in the same population.
source: Indeed, it is important to remember that different mechanisms leading to density dependence can occur simultaneously in the same population (Berec et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berec et al., 2007.

claim: In the models analyzed in this paper, conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality promotes species-rich communities in concert with negative density dependence driven by intraspecific competition for resources.
source: In the models analyzed in this paper, conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality promote species-rich communities in concert with negative density dependence (driven by intraspecific competition for resources), highlighting the necessity of dissecting the different density-dependent mechanisms acting simultaneously (as in Feldman and Morris, 2011; Bergamo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the study's models and supported by citations to Feldman and Morris, 2011 and Bergamo et al., 2020.

claim: Experimental manipulations of population density coupled with other treatments could prove useful to infer the nature and strength of density dependence and to define the underlying mechanisms.
source: In particular, experimental manipulations of population density coupled with other treatments (e.g. removal of predators/herbivores) could prove useful not only to infer the nature and strength of density dependence but also to define the underlying mechanisms (e.g. this is how negative density dependence in populations of reef fishes has been shown to be driven by competition and predation; Hixon, 1997; Forrester and Steele, 2000; Carr et al., 2002; Holbrook and Schmitt, 2002).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citations to studies on reef fishes.

claim: The causal link between conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality and species coexistence remains to be tested empirically.
source: In addition to the assessment of conspecific positive density dependence associated with reduced mortality in nature, the causal link between this form of density dependence and species coexistence remains to be tested empirically.
evidence: This identifies a gap between the theoretical findings and empirical validation.

claim: Imposing and amplifying conspecific positive density dependence in a controlled experimental setup could prove fruitful for testing the theoretical predictions.
source: Imposing and amplifying conspecific positive density dependence in a controlled experimental setup could prove fruitful (as in Williams and Levine, 2018, where negative density dependence was manipulated).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citation to Williams and Levine, 2018.

claim: In the theoretical models analyzed, conspecific positive density dependence strongly promoted the maintenance of species undergoing asymmetric reproductive interference.
source: In the theoretical models analyzed here, conspecific positive density dependence strongly promoted the maintenance of species undergoing asymmetric reproductive interference.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6d-f.

claim: Testing the theoretical predictions on empirical data in organisms involved in sexual interactions is encouraged.
source: I thus encourage testing the theoretical predictions presented in this paper on empirical data in organisms involved in such sexual interactions (e.g. Takafuji et al., 1997; Kishi et al., 2009; Takakura et al., 2009; Crowder et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: A variety of coexistence mechanisms operate simultaneously in nature.
source: Although a variety of coexistence mechanisms operate simultaneously in nature, these modeling results suggest that conspecific positive density dependence play a considerable role in structuring ecological communities.
evidence: This is general ecological knowledge.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence may play a considerable role in structuring ecological communities.
source: Although a variety of coexistence mechanisms operate simultaneously in nature, these modeling results suggest that conspecific positive density dependence play a considerable role in structuring ecological communities.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: Conspecific positive density dependence may have opposite effects on species coexistence depending on the underlying density-dependent mechanism.
source: Conspecific positive density dependence may have opposite effects on species coexistence depending on the underlying density-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the analytical and numerical results.
